title: Lobster Bisque
subtitle: Smooth, rich cream soup with lobster stock and sherry
excerpt: Lobster bisque is a smooth, rich cream soup built from lobster shells simmered into a stock, enriched with cream and a splash of sherry. It takes time but most of it is passive simmering. The result is an elegant, deeply flavoured soup for a special occasion.
sourceNotes: Lobster bisque is a classic French-American dish, particularly associated with New England coastal restaurants. The shell-stock method is the technique used across New England lobster shacks and fine dining alike.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make the bisque base up to a day ahead and refrigerate. Reheat gently and add the cream and lobster meat at the last minute.

content.text: Lobster bisque is built from the shells: they go into a pot with aromatics and wine to make a concentrated stock, which becomes the base of the soup. The stock is then enriched with cream and blended smooth. The lobster meat goes in at the end and barely cooks, just enough to warm through. The result is a soup that tastes entirely of the sea.

items.prepNote: cooked (about 600 g total), meat removed from claws, knuckles and tail; shells reserved

content.text: Melt {{unsalted-butter}} in a large heavy-based pan over medium-high heat. Add the reserved lobster shells and cook, stirring, for three to four minutes until they begin to colour and smell toasted. Add {{white-onion}}, {{celery}}, {{carrot}}, and {{garlic}} and cook for five minutes more until the vegetables soften.

Stir in {{tomato-puree}} and cook for two minutes. Add {{dry-sherry}} and {{white-wine-dry}}, increase the heat, and let the alcohol cook off for two minutes. Pour in {{stock-fish}}, add {{bay-leaf}} and {{paprika-smoked}}, and bring to a gentle simmer. Cook for 30 minutes.

Remove the shells and bay leaves. Transfer the solids and liquid in batches to a blender and blend until completely smooth. Pass through a fine-mesh sieve back into the pan, pressing firmly to extract everything.

Stir in {{double-cream}} and bring to a very gentle simmer over medium-low heat. Season with {{sea-salt-fine}} and {{cayenne-pepper}}. Add the lobster meat and warm through for two to three minutes, just enough to heat it, not to cook it further. Serve in warmed bowls.

items.symptom: The bisque is thin and watery
items.cause: Stock not reduced enough, or too much fish stock used.
items.fix: After straining, boil the bisque base (before adding cream) to reduce by a quarter. The cream will also thicken it; adjust the consistency to taste.

items.symptom: The bisque tastes flat and lacks depth
items.cause: Shells not toasted, or tomato purée not cooked out.
items.fix: The shell-toasting step is where the deep colour and flavour come from. Cook them until they are really starting to colour. Cook the tomato purée until it darkens to a brick red.

items.symptom: The bisque tastes too much of cream
items.cause: Too much cream relative to the stock base.
items.fix: The base should be intensely flavoured before the cream goes in. Start with 150 ml of cream and add more to taste. The cream enriches but should not dilute.
Add the lobster meat off the heat, or at the lowest possible simmer, for two minutes only. Already-cooked lobster only needs warming through.

content.text: Lobster bisque is one of the signature dishes of New England coastal cuisine, where lobster is both a staple and a luxury. The shell-stock technique, adapted from French classical cooking, turns the by-products of a lobster meal (the shells, the roe, the bits too fiddly to eat cleanly) into the foundation of the soup. It's a dish that rewards patience: the longer the stock simmers, the richer the result.
